newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka's Galle port to get $350 mln facelift.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka's Galle port to get $350 mln facelift.

text.p: A British-Chinese consortium, led by Mott Macdonald of Britain, has proposed a $350 million plan to develop Sri Lanka's ancient Galle harbour into a modern trans-shipment port, officials said on Wednesday.

"The new port will have five berths with a capacity of a million containers a year," Suppiah Kandasamy, the chairman of the consortium, said after handing over the project feasibility study to Ports and Shipping Minister Mohamed Ashraff.
"Mother ships from the West coming past Aden can stop at Galle where trans-shipment will take place instead of going on to Singapore," he told Reuters.

The consortium, apart from Mott Macdonald, consists of three Chinese firms -- Wuhun China International, Harbour Engineering Investigation Corporation and Harbour Construction and Design. The three Chinese firms are being coordinated by China-Lanka International, and the project has been promoted by Kandasmay's Construction and Personnel Services.
The consortium expects trans-shipment traffic to account for 80 percent of the volume in the new Galle port, half of which would be from the Indian sub-continent, he said.
Trans-shipment occurs when a vessel discharges cargo at an intermediate port and the goods are unloaded to another ship bound for the final destination.

Colombo port, south Asia's trans-shipment hub on the island's west coast, is seen nearing its capacity of 1.6 million containers in 1997, having handled some 1.3 million units last year, up 28 percent from 1995.
The increase was mainly in trans-shipment traffic, which came after the realingment of container shipping alliances in the middle of last year, port officials said.

Colombo port is now in talks with a consortium led by the Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co. to build a new, deep-draft container terminal to expand capacity by two million containers a year.
Galle, 115 km (70 miles) south of Colombo, is considered a better location for trans-shipment than Colombo because it is near the main international shipping route across the Indian Ocean.

The modernisation of Galle, under the consortium's build, operate and transfer project, could help ease pressure on Colombo port and allow big container ships to save eight hours by not deviating to Colombo.
Kandasamy said it would take three years to build the new Galle port and nine years to recover the investment.
The port, which now has a draft of only 7.3 metres, will be dredged to accomodate bigger ships, while a new container terminal-cum-breakwater will be built across the bay.
The government will inherit the investment in the project, including infrastructure and equipment, after 25 years.
Galle was Sri Lanka's main port, through which commodities such as tea and cinnamon were exported, until the late 19th century when British colonial rulers built the harbour at Colombo.
Galle's importance then faded and containerisation of shipping led to its further neglect as Colombo emerged as a hub, with trans-shipment accounting for 70 percent of throughput.
Few ships use Galle today although it remains a popular port of call for round-the-world yacht races.
Only 95,000 tonnes of cargo, mostly clinker for a nearby cement factory, and flour, passed through Galle in 1995 in comparison to Colombo's 14.7 million tonnes.
